Faireez · Marketplace

You can't sell what people can't picture - so we built a store that taught them.

Services
Product UX · Strategy
Client
Faireez
Platform
iOS · Web
Method
6Qs (Eyal David)

Faireez puts a housekeeper - a "fairy" - in the lobbies of luxury buildings in New York and Miami. The promise is granular: book her for just the dishes, just the laundry, just the living room. Early on, almost no one did.

We'd packaged the service into modular bundles, but residents couldn't even form the thought that a single chore was bookable. Before redesigning anything, I ran the problem through a disciplined set of questions - the 6Qs - and the answer reframed the whole project.

Background

the full range

Faireez is on-demand home help, staffed by a fairy stationed in the building's lobby. From the fridge to the laundry to the windows, there's almost no household chore she can't take.

The original model sold all of it as modular packages - pick a tier, get a set of tasks. It read clearly to us, who already understood the product. It did not read to a resident who'd never encountered à-la-carte home help.

The friction

two problems, one root

Residents couldn't conceive of booking around a single task - and the packages didn't fix it, because the barrier was never price or tiering, it was comprehension.

Meanwhile the fairy sat in the lobby with idle hours: demand we were generating but not capturing. So before touching the UI, I ran it through the 6Qs.

Getting the why right - the 6Qs

A discipline I picked up from Eyal David: define the real question before you design the answer.

Q1What's the real problem?

Residents can't picture booking a single chore. It's a comprehension gap - not pricing, not packaging.

Q2What does the data say?

With modular packages live, single-task bookings were near zero. Research was blunt: people had never experienced à-la-carte home help, so they couldn't imagine it.

Q3What's the hypothesis?

Give single tasks their own storefront - a Marketplace with bundles and flash deals - and people will grasp it by seeing it. Single-visit bookings will rise.

Q6How do we measure it?

Single-visit bookings as a share of all orders - plus Marketplace entry→checkout and reduced fairy idle time.

Q4 (impact) and Q5 (audience) rounded out the brief. Read the 6Qs method by Eyal David ↗

The insight

The problem wasn't packaging. It was imagination.

You can't buy what you can't picture - and people weren't rejecting single-task booking, they simply couldn't form the thought.

So the fix wasn't a better explanation. It was to show the concept instead of describing it: give single tasks a literal storefront, where "Do My Dishes - $15" sitting on a shelf makes the idea self-evident.

The solution

a store you already know how to use

The Marketplace. Single tasks became individual products - organize the fridge, do the dishes, replace the sheets - each a concrete, low-commitment "yes," bookable one-time or on a schedule.

Related tasks grouped into bundles. Flash deals with a live countdown pulled residents into the space and gave them a reason to look. And we taught the concept in their own language: just like ordering food - choose the task you need and get it.

One mechanism, two wins: it taught people that a single chore is bookable, and it converted the fairy's idle lobby time into discounted, on-the-spot work.

The Marketplace - single chores added one-time or regularly; one chore, one screen, one tap.

Flash deals filled idle lobby hours and drove people in - and the idea was taught like ordering food.

The result

Shown, not told - and people started buying the thing they couldn't picture.

Once the concept lived as a storefront instead of an explanation, it clicked: single-visit bookings rose significantly, and residents began composing their own help, one chore at a time.

The lesson was never in a tooltip or an onboarding flow. It was in the shape of the product itself.
